docs.title: Metagenomic Data Analysis of Microbial Communities (MGMC01)
Course overview
docs.text:
Course flyer

This course covers the metagenomics data analysis workflow from data generation to downstream analysis. Participants explore the tools to manage, share, analyze and interpret metagenomics data. The content includes issues of data quality control and how to process the data until publication.

Both targeted marker-gene (e.g., 16S) and whole-genome shotgun (WGS) approaches are covered. Discussions also explore considerations when selecting the sequencing options (long or short reads), exploring targeted data to OTUs or ASVs, assembling and binning metagenomics data, available tools, and the downstream analyses that can be carried out.

docs.title: What you’ll learn
docs.text:
After this course, you will be able to:

  • Explain the core concepts of metagenomics and design a study (replication, controls, sampling, sequencing strategy), distinguishing targeted from shotgun approaches.
  • Assess the quality of raw sequencing reads (Illumina short reads, PacBio long reads) and interpret FastQC reports.
  • Describe marker gene selection (16S, ITS), primer design and PCR biases, and contrast OTU- and ASV-based workflows.
  • Process targeted 16S amplicon (eDNA) reads with DADA2 and carry out a downstream analysis with PhyloSeq: rarefaction, α- and β-diversity, geographic mapping and LEfSe.
  • Explain how sequencing depth and coverage shape shotgun metagenomics, and how k-mer- and alignment-based classifiers work.
  • Understand the steps of a reference-based metagenomics pipeline (host removal, taxonomic classification with Kraken2/Bracken).
  • Run a Nextflow-based metagenomics pipeline end-to-end.
  • Visualize taxonomic profiles interactively with Krona plots and Pavian.
  • Carry out a downstream compositional analysis with Phyloseq: α- and β-diversity, ordination and network analysis.
  • Explain the principles of de novo metagenome assembly and evaluate assembly quality.
  • Describe binning strategies and their role in recovering MAGs.
  • Perform an integral analysis of Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs): quality assessment with BUSCO/CheckM2 and BIgMAG, metabolic potential with KEGG Decoder, functional annotation (COG, CAZymes, biosynthetic gene clusters), genome visualization with Proksee and pangenome analysis.
  • Apply the FAIR principles and reproducible-analysis practices (workflow managers, containers) to metagenomic datasets.

docs.title: Course goal
docs.text:
This course walks you through a complete metagenomics analysis across five days. On Day 1 you will learn the core concepts of metagenomics, study-design considerations and sequencing technologies, and how to assess the quality of raw sequencing reads (both short, Illumina-style reads and long, PacBio-style reads) with FastQC. On Day 2 we cover targeted marker-gene sequencing: after the theory (marker gene selection, primer design, PCR biases, OTUs vs ASVs), you will process 16S amplicon (eDNA) reads with DADA2 (filtering, error correction, merging, chimera removal, taxonomy assignment), followed by a downstream analysis with PhyloSeq (rarefaction, α- and β-diversity, barplots, geographic localisation and a LEfSe analysis). On Day 3 we move to shotgun (whole-genome) metagenomics: how depth and coverage shape the analysis, k-mer vs alignment-based read classification, and a Nextflow-based pipeline that performs host removal with Bowtie2, taxonomic classification with Kraken2/Bracken and visualization with Krona plots. You will then compare samples with Pavian and build a Phyloseq object from the pipeline output to explore α- and β-diversity, ordination and network analyses. On Day 4 we deal with assembly and binning: principles of de novo metagenome assembly, the challenges of community complexity and strain microdiversity, and the binning strategies (MetaBAT2, MaxBin2 and friends) used by nf-core/mag to recover Metagenome-Assembled Genomes. On Day 5 we close the analysis arc with the integral analysis of the recovered MAGs — quality assessment with BUSCO/CheckM2 and the BIgMAG dashboard, metabolic potential with KEGG Decoder, functional annotation with COGclassifier, dbCAN3 and antiSMASH, genome visualization with Proksee and a pangenome comparison with Roary/Phandango — before zooming out to FAIR data and reproducible analyses with workflow managers and containers.

By the end of the course, you will have run a complete metagenomics workflow from raw reads to biological interpretation, and you will be able to interpret the outputs at each stage: FastQC reports, DADA2 denoising outputs, Kraken2/Bracken reports, Krona plots, Pavian comparisons, Phyloseq figures and MAG quality/functional annotation outputs.

docs.title: Session 1 - Introduction to metagenomics, goals and opportunities
What is metagenomics?
docs.text:
Metagenomics is the study of genetic material recovered directly from environmental or clinical samples, without the need to isolate and cultivate individual microorganisms. By sequencing all the DNA (or RNA) present in a sample, metagenomics gives us access to the composition and functional potential of whole microbial communities — bacteria, archaea, fungi, viruses and eukaryotic microbes — in their ecological context.

The term metagenomics was coined in the late 1990s, but the field took off with the advent of high-throughput sequencing: culture-independent approaches suddenly made it possible to explore the so-called “unculturable majority” — the estimated >99% of microbial species that have never been grown in pure culture. From the first 16S rRNA gene surveys to today’s whole-genome shotgun sequencing, metagenomics has become a cornerstone of microbial ecology, clinical diagnostics, biotechnology and planetary health monitoring.

docs.title: Goals and opportunities
docs.text:
Depending on the question at hand, a metagenomics study can pursue different goals:

  • Who is there? — taxonomic profiling of the community (which organisms, and in which proportions).
  • What can they do? — functional profiling (which metabolic pathways, enzymes or traits are encoded by the community).
  • Who is doing what? — combining taxonomy and function, e.g. through metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) or metatranscriptomics.

These questions arise in a wide variety of fields: environmental studies (soil, water, extreme environments, biogeochemical cycles), clinical applications (gut microbiome, infectious disease, antimicrobial resistance), and biotechnological opportunities (enzyme discovery, bioremediation, agriculture, industrial fermentation).

docs.title: Study design considerations
docs.text:
Before any sequencing takes place, a good metagenomics study is designed on paper. The most common pitfalls in microbiome research originate in the experimental design rather than in the analysis, so it is worth pausing here:

Questions to ask yourself before starting

  • Biological question: which comparison (conditions, time points, gradients) will answer it?
  • Replication: how many biological replicates per group? (Under-replicated designs cannot support statistical testing.)
  • Controls: negative controls (extraction blanks, PCR blanks to detect reagent contamination) and positive controls (mock communities to assess accuracy).
  • Confounding variables: batch effects, extraction kits, sequencing runs, storage time — are they balanced across groups?
  • Sampling and storage: how were the samples collected, preserved and extracted? The protocol strongly shapes the resulting community profile.
  • Sequencing strategy: targeted (amplicon) or shotgun? Short or long reads? How deep do I need to sequence?

docs.title: Sequencing technologies: short and long reads
docs.text:
Sequencing technologies have evolved to provide us with different types of reads. Each type has its own applications and considerations for QC, and the choice of platform influences every subsequent step of the analysis:

  • Short reads: generated by platforms like Illumina, they are typically 75–300 bp in length. They offer high throughput and very low per-base error rates, making them the workhorse of both amplicon and shotgun metagenomics. Their main limitation is that the reads are much shorter than most microbial genomes and genes, which complicates the reconstruction of complete genomes and of repetitive or strain-variable regions.
  • Long reads: produced by platforms such as PacBio and Oxford Nanopore, they can be over 10 kb in length (and now routinely beyond 100 kb). They span complete operons and even complete bacterial genomes, which greatly helps assembly and the resolution of strains and plasmids — at the cost of higher per-base error rates (although modern chemistries and consensus methods have largely closed this gap) and, historically, lower throughput.
Not either/or

Increasingly, studies combine both technologies in hybrid assemblies, using short reads for accuracy and long reads for continuity. Throughout this course you will work mainly with Illumina short reads, but the QC principles you learn apply to long reads as well — you will see PacBio data in the practical below.

docs.title: Practical Activity: Design Your Own Metagenomics Study
docs.text:
Objective: Design a metagenomics study to answer a scientific question, considering sampling strategy, experimental design, sequencing technology, and potential limitations.

Activity

Read your assigned scenario, use the provided questions to guide you through your mission and search for relevant literature for your scenario. Prepare a 5-min presentation describing what you found in terms of the problem, the proposed experiments and methodology and the expected outcomes.

Scenario 1

Scenario 1 — Rice Straw Decomposition

Your mission: Help farmers understand how microorganisms contribute to rice straw decomposition.

Rice straw contains cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. A research team wants to determine whether applying a microbial inoculant improves decomposition and changes the microbial community.

Topic Questions Research question What hypothesis would you test? Study design Which treatments, controls, replicates, and sampling time points would you include? Sequencing Would you choose amplicon sequencing, short-read shotgun, or long-read sequencing? Why? Expected results How would you identify microorganisms with potential lignocellulose-degrading capabilities? Scenario 2

Scenario 2 — Antibiotic Resistance in Wastewater

Your mission: Investigate whether wastewater treatment reduces the environmental spread of antibiotic resistance.

Hospital wastewater may contain antibiotic resistance genes and resistant bacteria. Researchers want to compare wastewater before and after treatment and investigate which microorganisms carry resistance genes.

Topic Questions Research question What would you measure to evaluate changes in antibiotic resistance? Study design Where would you sample, and how would you account for temporal variation? Sequencing Which approach would help identify resistance genes and link them to microbial genomes? Expected results Would detecting fewer resistance genes prove that resistant bacteria have been eliminated? What additional evidence would you need? Scenario 3

Scenario 3 — Diet and the Human Gut Microbiome

Your mission: Investigate whether a high-fiber diet changes the gut microbiome.

A research team wants to determine whether a high-fiber dietary intervention changes microbial composition and functional potential, and whether these changes are associated with improved metabolic health.

Topic Questions Research question What hypothesis would you test? Study design How would you compare participants and account for individual differences? Sequencing Would you choose amplicon sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, or metatranscriptomics? Expected results Can DNA sequencing alone demonstrate that microbial genes are actively expressed or that the microbiome caused a health improvement? Scenario 4

Scenario 4 — Discovering Industrial Enzymes

Your mission: Discover microbial enzymes that could improve the conversion of agricultural residues into valuable products.

A biotechnology company wants to find novel enzymes from microorganisms living in environments such as compost, hot springs, and industrial wastewater. The goal is to identify promising candidates for industrial applications.

Topic Questions Research question Which environments would you sample, and why? Study design How would you select samples and biological replicates? Sequencing Which sequencing technology would best support enzyme discovery and linking genes to microbial genomes? Expected results How would you distinguish a predicted enzyme function from experimentally demonstrated activity? Final Challenge: Your Budget Is Cut by 50%!

In each case, revise the study design.

  • What would you prioritize: more biological replicates, deeper sequencing, or additional sampling time points?
  • What would you sacrifice, and how would this affect your conclusions?
  • What is the most important scientific question your revised study could still answer?

docs.title: Session 2 - Quality control and contamination assessment
Overview of quality control
docs.text:
Quality control (QC) is a critical step in any NGS workflow, and the metagenomics workflow is no exception. It ensures that the data used for analysis is of high quality and free from errors that could compromise the results. In this session, we will discuss the importance of QC and introduce the tools we will use to assess and improve the quality of our sequencing reads.

Poor read quality, adapter contamination, PCR duplicates or foreign DNA (host, phiX spike-in, reagent contaminants) left in the data will propagate through every downstream step: biased diversity estimates, false taxonomic assignments, fragmented assemblies and unreliable MAGs. QC is thus not a formality but the foundation of every analysis in this course.

docs.title: Quality assessment tools
docs.text:
We will use FastQC to assess the quality of our reads:

  • FastQC: A widely used tool for quality checking of raw sequence data coming from high throughput sequencing pipelines.

FastQC output

Discuss the results and compare cleaned vs raw reads:

  • Are the cleaned reads in sufficient good quality?

  • Do you see an impact of the cleaning?

After cleaning Module Status What it shows Interpretation Per base sequence content ❌ FAIL ~100% single-base spikes at positions 1–9 (G-A-C-T-A-C-…-G-G-G), then irregular swings along the read Expected for amplicons: all reads cover the same region, so base composition is fixed at each position. The primer is likely still present and should be removed (e.g. cutadapt) before ASV/OTU calling. Per sequence GC content ⚠️ WARNING Narrow peak at ~57–58% GC (narrower than the theoretical curve), small shoulder at ~47–48% Expected for amplicons: reads come from one short, conserved region, so GC is uniform. The shoulder may reflect lower-GC taxa. Smooth shape, so no contamination signal. Sequence duplication levels ❌ FAIL Only 8.66% of reads would remain after deduplication Expected for amplicons: abundant taxa produce identical sequences. Do not deduplicate, since abundance information would be lost. Overrepresented sequences ❌ FAIL Top sequence = 2-4% of reads. Dozens of near-identical entries (0.5–3% each), all starting GACTAC…GGGTATCTAATCC…, labelled “No Hit” Expected for amplicons: these are the primer region plus variants from different taxa (and some sequencing errors). “No Hit” means they are not in FastQC’s contaminant list, so the primer is not recognised.

docs.text:
Download the following FastQC files:

  • Single-genome reads

Amplicon sequencing vs WGS of single-genome

  • What are the differences?
Amplicon sequencing vs WGS of single-genome Module 16S amplicon Single genome Why they differ Basic statistics 294,158 reads, fixed 160 bp, 54% GC 957,850 reads, 35–151 bp, 70% GC Amplicons give uniform length and a GC value set by the 16S region. The genome’s GC (70%) is a property of the organism (a high-GC genome). Per base sequence content ❌ FAIL: ~100% single-base spikes at positions 1–9, irregular swings along the whole read ❌ FAIL: bias only in the first ~10–15 bp, then flat lines (C ≈ G ≈ 35%, A ≈ T ≈ 15%) Same flag, different cause. In the amplicon sample every read starts with the primer and the whole read is the same region. In the single-genome sample the flat profile after ~15 bp is what a random genome fragment library should look like. The 5′ bias is typical of library-prep bias (e.g. transposase/tagmentation or priming), not a primer. Per sequence GC content ⚠️ WARNING: narrow peak at ~57–58% plus a shoulder ⚠️ WARNING: single peak at ~71–72%, slightly taller and narrower than theoretical The peak in the amplicon sequencing is narrow because all reads are one conserved region. The one in the single-genome sample is a single smooth peak, consistent with one genome and no obvious contamination. The warning is minor. Sequence length distribution ✅ PASS (159–161 bp) ⚠️ WARNING (35–151 bp, most reads at 151) The single-genome reads were trimmed (adapters/quality), so the lengths vary. Amplicon reads were trimmed to one fixed length. Sequence duplication levels ❌ FAIL: 8.66% remain after deduplication ✅ PASS: 88.21% remain after deduplication Amplicons are duplicated by design. A single genome sampled at modest depth should give mostly unique reads. Overrepresented sequences ❌ FAIL: primer-derived sequences at 0.5–4% each ✅ PASS: none Only the amplicon library has a few sequences dominating the reads.

docs.title: Tips: FastQC output explained
docs.text:
Reading the report at a glance

Each module is flagged pass (green), warning (yellow) or fail (red). A single warning does not automatically mean the data are bad, meaning that modules must be interpreted together; always compare raw vs cleaned reads. In metagenomics, some deviations (e.g. GC content or duplication) are expected because a sample contains many organisms.

The most relevant modules to look at when assessing the quality of your reads:

Module What it shows What to look for Per Sequence Quality Scores Distribution of the average quality score over all reads. A second peak at low quality reveals a subset of poor-quality reads. Per Base Sequence Content Proportion of each base (A, T, C, G) at each position across all reads. A non-random or strongly biased profile suggests contamination or a library-construction bias. Per Sequence GC Content Observed GC distribution compared with a theoretical distribution. A shifted or secondary peak can indicate contamination or an unexpected organism. Per Base N Content Proportion of bases called as N at each position (undetermined bases). A high or rising N content points to failing base calls and poor quality. Sequence Length Distribution Distribution of read lengths. Unexpected lengths may reflect trimming problems, degradation or adapter read-through. Sequence Duplication Levels Percentage of reads that are duplicates of other reads. High duplication suggests PCR amplification bias or low-complexity libraries. Overrepresented Sequences Sequences appearing more often than expected. Can be adapter, primer, rRNA or a contaminant — or genuinely abundant biological sequence. Adapter Content Presence of adapter sequences along the reads. Adapter content rising towards the read end means trimming is needed. Kmer Content Kmers (short nucleotide sequences) that are overrepresented at particular positions. Position-specific anomalies can indicate contamination or biases.

Some modules are expected to warn in metagenomics

Duplication levels, GC content and per-base sequence content can look unusual simply because many genomes are mixed together. Interpret these modules in the context of the sample type, and give more weight to quality scores, adapter content and overrepresented sequences.

docs.text:
Work through the questions below. Open the hint only after you have looked at your reports.

1. Did the cleaning improve the quality of the reads?

In which module(s) do you see the impact? Compare the raw and cleaned reports side by side.

Hint

Focus on adapter content, per-base sequence content and overrepresented sequences. Quality scores and N content often improve too.

2. What are the main differences between Illumina 16S short reads, PacBio long reads and metagenomics WGS in terms of quality?

Compare the three datasets you analysed.

Hint

Consider read length, per-base error profiles, duplication levels and how many organisms contribute to the signal.

3. How would you proceed if a sample fails the quality control?

Think about the decision tree before reaching for a tool.

Hint

First identify which module fails and why. Then consider trimming/filtering, removing contamination (host, phiX, adapters), re-extracting or re-sequencing. Document the decision and the parameters used.

4. Where does contamination typically enter a metagenomics experiment, and which controls would you use to detect it?

Trace the sample from collection to sequencing.

Hint

Sources include reagents, extraction kits, PCR, the laboratory environment and cross-contamination between samples. Use extraction blanks, PCR blanks and mock communities as negative and positive controls.

docs.title: Principles of amplicon-based sequencing
docs.text: Targeted (amplicon) metagenomics does not sequence all the DNA in a sample. Instead, it amplifies and sequences a specific marker gene present in all members of a target group, using PCR with primers that flank a conserved region. The variable regions between the primers then serve as a molecular fingerprint for taxonomic identification. Because only a tiny fraction of the community DNA is sequenced, amplicon approaches are cheap, tolerate low DNA yields and can reach very high numbers of samples. This great advantage comes at the price of capturing who is there, but generally not what they can do.

docs.title: Marker gene selection
docs.text:
The choice of marker gene defines the resolution and the scope of the study:

  • 16S rRNA gene: the standard marker for bacteria and archaea. Combines conserved regions (for universal primer binding) with nine variable regions (V1–V9) carrying taxonomic signal. Typical amplicons target V3–V4, V4 or V1–V2, ~250–450 bp.
  • ITS (Internal Transcribed Spacer): the official marker for fungi. Much more variable than 16S, which gives excellent species-level resolution but makes reference databases and primer specificity more challenging.
  • Other markers: 18S rRNA for eukaryotes, rpoB/gyrB for higher resolution in specific groups, or multi-marker panels.

docs.title: Primer design, PCR biases and library preparation
docs.text:
Every PCR step imprints itself on the data, and understanding these biases is essential to interpret the results correctly:

  • Primer coverage and specificity: no primer pair is truly universal. Mismatches at the binding site cause systematic under-detection (or complete missing) of some taxa; in silico coverage tests against reference databases should guide primer choice.
  • Amplification bias: primers do not amplify all targets with equal efficiency; GC content, secondary structures and template length all play a role.
  • Chimeras: partially extended molecules from one template can prime on another during later PCR cycles, creating artificial sequences that must be removed computationally.
  • Tag switching / index hopping: sample cross-contamination on the sequencer, mitigated by unique dual indexes.
  • Library preparation strategies: two-stage (2-step) PCR protocols (amplicon PCR + indexing PCR) are standard for Illumina sequencing; amplicon length must match the chosen read length so that paired reads overlap (e.g. V3–V4 ~460 bp with 2×250 bp reads).

Design checklist

Whenever you design your own amplicon study, it is worthy to check:

  • Which marker and variable region? Which primer pair (and its coverage)?

  • How many negatives and mock communities? How many biological replicates?

docs.title: OTUs vs ASVs
docs.text:
Two paradigms exist to turn raw amplicon reads into discrete features:

OTUs (Operational Taxonomic Units) ASVs (Amplicon Sequence Variants) Inference Greedy clustering of reads at a similarity threshold (typically 97%) Model-based denoising of exact sequences (error model per run) Resolution Genus-ish; single-nucleotide variants collapsed Single-nucleotide resolution Reproducibility Depends on the dataset and algorithm (pipeline-specific) Exact sequences, that make them comparable across studies Noise handling Abundance filters (e.g. remove singletons) Probabilistic error and chimera removal Example tools UPARSE, VSEARCH, mothur DADA2, UNOISE3, Deblur

Modern amplicon workflows (and this course) use ASVs: they are more precise, reproducible and better suited for combining studies.

In Session 4 we will process real 16S reads into ASVs with DADA2 and interpret the resulting community tables ecologically.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: This session introduces a targeted-amplicon (16S rRNA) analysis of environmental DNA (eDNA) samples collected along the Danube river, using the R package DADA2 and the downstream analysis toolbox PhyloSeq. You start from raw Illumina paired-end reads, go through the classical denoising pipeline, and finish with ecological and statistical interpretation of the recovered ASVs (Amplicon Sequence Variants).

docs.title: Part I - Sequence processing with DADA2
docs.text: For the first part we will process the 24 samples of 16S amplicon reads (2×250 bp paired-end Illumina reads) that have already been trimmed of primers and adapters by cutadapt. The workflow follows the steps of the DADA2 tutorial: quality assessment, filtering, learning the error rates, denoising, merging paired reads, chimera removal and taxonomy assignment. DADA2 implements a model-based error-correction method that resolves Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) differing by just a single nucleotide.

docs.title: Filtering and truncation of reads
docs.text:
We filter the reads with the standard parameters: maxN=0 (DADA2 requires no Ns), truncQ=2, rm.phix=TRUE and maxEE=2. The maxEE parameter sets the maximum number of “expected errors” allowed in a read, which is a better filter than simply averaging quality scores. In this case we do not truncate the reads (truncLen=0) but in other cases it could be adjusted, e.g. truncLen=c(220,160).

docs.title: Learn the error rates and correct the reads
docs.text:
Slow step

This part is relatively slow (about 5 min on a laptop).

DADA2 learns the error rates from the data itself using a machine-learning algorithm, once for the forward and once for the reverse reads:

RStudio

Learn the error rates
errF <- learnErrors(filtFs, multithread=TRUE)
errR <- learnErrors(filtRs, multithread=TRUE)

plotErrors(errF, nominalQ=TRUE)

Estimated errors

Estimated error rates for the forward reads. The black line (learned) fits the observed points well.

Estimated error rates for the reverse reads.

Error rates

The error rates for each possible transition (A->C, A->G, …) are shown. Points are the observed error rates for each consensus quality score. The black line shows the estimated error rates after convergence of the machine-learning algorithm. The red line shows the error rates expected under the nominal definition of the Q-score.

Everything looks reasonable, so we can proceed with confidence and apply the core sample-inference algorithm:

RStudio

Denoise the reads

dadaFs <- dada(filtFs, err=errF, multithread=TRUE, pool="pseudo") # On Windows set multithread=FALSE
dadaRs <- dada(filtRs, err=errR, multithread=TRUE, pool="pseudo")
dadaFs[[1]]

152 sequence variants were inferred from 4774 input unique sequences.
Key parameters: OMEGA_A = 1e-40, OMEGA_C = 1e-40, BAND_SIZE = 16
Pooling samples

By default, the dada function processes each sample independently. Pooling information across samples can increase sensitivity to sequence variants that may be present at very low frequencies in multiple samples. dada(..., pool=TRUE) performs standard pooled processing, whereas dada(..., pool="pseudo") (used above) shares information between samples while processing them independently, approximating pooled inference in linear time. docs.title: Day 3 - Shotgun metagenomics: classification and downstream analysis
Learning outcomes
docs.text:
After having completed this chapter you will be able to:

  • Explain the principles of shotgun (whole-genome) metagenomics and how library preparation, sequencing depth and coverage shape the analysis.
  • Distinguish k-mer-based from alignment-based approaches for read-level taxonomic classification.
  • Distinguish taxonomic classification (per-read assignment) from taxonomic profiling (community composition estimates).
  • Run a reference-based metagenomics pipeline (Bowtie2 → Kraken2 → Bracken → Krona) with Nextflow.
  • Explore taxonomic profiles per sample with interactive Krona plots.
  • Compare samples with Pavian using Kraken2 reports.
  • Build a Phyloseq object from a BIOM file and sample metadata.
  • Estimate α- and β-diversity, and run ordination and network analyses.

docs.title: Whole genome sequencing and taxonomic classification
Principles of shotgun metagenomic sequencing
docs.text: Unlike targeted amplicon sequencing (Day 2), shotgun metagenomics sequences all the DNA present in a sample at once. The community DNA is fragmented (physically or enzymatically), sequencing adapters are ligated to both ends of every fragment, and the library is sequenced from both sides. No prior knowledge of which organisms are present is required, so the approach captures bacteria, archaea, fungi, viruses and host DNA. Crucially, it delivers functional information (genes, pathways, MAGs) in addition to taxonomy.

docs.title: Library preparation, depth and coverage
docs.text:
Several design decisions determine what a shotgun dataset can resolve:

  • Library preparation: typically PCR-free or low-cycle protocols are preferred to avoid amplification bias; paired-end short reads (2×150 bp) are the standard, while long-read libraries (PacBio, Nanopore) improve continuity at higher cost and error rate. Host DNA depletion or methylation-based enrichment can be used when the microbial fraction is low (e.g. clinical samples).
  • Sequencing depth: how many reads are generated per sample. Shallow shotgun (~1 Gb) supports family-level profiling; deep sequencing (5–20+ Gb) is needed for strain resolution, assembly and MAG recovery.
  • Coverage: the number of times a genome is sequenced, which depends on sequencing depth and on the relative abundance of the organism in the community. A genome at 1% relative abundance in a 10 Gb run receives only ~100 Mb of reads (often not enough to assemble). Abundance and genome size therefore jointly determine which members of a community can be recovered as MAGs.
  • Community complexity: diverse environments (soil, marine) dilute the coverage of individual genomes, while low-complexity communities (gut, enrichment cultures) are more amenable to assembly and binning (Day 4).

docs.title: Read-based taxonomic classification
docs.text:
Before dealing with assemblies (Days 4–5), the fastest way to obtain a community profile is to classify individual reads against a reference database. Two families of methods dominate:

  • k-mer (hashing)-based: each read is split into k-mers, and the taxonomy of the k-mers (precomputed from a reference genome database) votes for the most likely origin of the read. Extremely fast and memory-efficient for large databases. Examples: Kraken2, KrakenUniq, Centrifuge.
  • alignment-based: reads (or their translated products) are aligned with BLAST or DIAMOND against reference sequences; taxonomies are then transferred from the best hits. Slower, but sensitive for divergent sequences and protein-level (functional) assignment. Examples: DIAMOND+MEGAN, BLAST-based classifiers.
  • marker-gene-based: only reads matching clade-specific marker genes are used (e.g. MetaPhlAn). Compact, but limited to the markers represented in the database.

The database is the analysis

All reference-based methods are only as good as their database: incomplete or mislabelled references produce false positives and missing taxa. Always record which database version you used.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
For this course, we propose to wrap with Nextflow the protocol published by Jennifer Lu et al. (2022). The wrapped workflow is called TaxoFlow and is designed as follows:

Reference-based metagenomics workflow used throughout this session.

As you can see from the picture, the input is FASTQ files from one or multiple samples, then it performs a host removal with Bowtie2 by aligning the reads against an indexed reference genome to carry out the taxonomic classification with Kraken2 afterwards. Taking the output from Kraken2, a Bayesian species abundance re-estimation is achieved with Bracken, and Krona plots are generated using the Bracken output to visualize interactively the relative abundance of each annotated species. If multiple samples are used as input to the pipeline, the bracken reports will be concatenated and converted into a Biological Observation Matrix (BIOM) file. Finally, the BIOM file will be first converted in a Phyloseq object, and this object will be further processed to generate absolute plots, estimate both α and β-diversity and perform a network analysis; this information will be presented in a final report.html.

docs.title: Phyloseq object
docs.text:
First, download the files found here and place them in a proper local directory (i.e. ~/Desktop/taxoflow).

Now, let’s create the Phyloseq object using the BIOM file generated by the pipeline and the experiment metadata. We are going to manipulate a bit the object to add the names of the taxonomic ranks, complete the species names and subset it to have only two conditions.

RStudio

Build the Phyloseq object
library(phyloseq)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# change the PATH according to your settings
setwd("~/Desktop/taxoflow")
tab_sam = read.csv("test_sheet.csv")
data_biom <- import_biom("merged.biom")
data_biom@tax_table@.Data <- substring(data_biom@tax_table@.Data, 4)
colnames(data_biom@tax_table@.Data) <- c("Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species")

tax_table_df <- as.data.frame(tax_table(data_biom))

# Modify the species column to include genus
tax_table_df$Species <- paste(tax_table_df$Genus, tax_table_df$Species, sep = " ")

# Update the taxonomy table in the phyloseq object
tax_table(data_biom) <- as.matrix(tax_table_df)

# Phyloseq object with only Bacteria
data_biom_bact <- subset_taxa(data_biom, Kingdom == "Bacteria")

samples_df <- tab_sam %>%
tibble::column_to_rownames("Name")
samples = sample_data(samples_df)
otu_inf = data_biom_bact@otu_table
phy_inf = data_biom_bact@tax_table
merged <- phyloseq(otu_inf, phy_inf, samples)

two_sample_data <- subset_samples(merged, Group == "Cont" | Group == "Unenriched")
two_sample_data

tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 4322 taxa by 7 taxonomic ranks ]

docs.title: β-Diversity
docs.text: β-Diversity measures how different two or more communities are, either in their composition (richness) or in the abundance of the organisms that compose it (abundance). To perform the analysis, we need to use dimensionality reduction techniques which enable comparisons in a space closer to our understanding (up to 3 dimensions). First, let’s create a heatmap that includes an ordination-based ordering of samples or taxa with a Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix as input for the ordination method (PCoA):

docs.text:

            taxa.label = "Phylum",

docs.title: Statistical modelling
docs.text:
For our simple scenario Control vs Unenriched samples, we will fit a linear model per taxon at each rank using the microViz R package.

Important considerations:

  • We will perform modelling a each taxonomic rank, and thus this requires quite some computation power. Also, this means that we need to adjust p-values to control False Discovery Rate.

  • We will filter the data since it’s less likely that we are interested in rare taxa, and models of rare taxon abundances are more likely to be unreliable. Reducing the the number of taxa modelled also makes visualising the results easier!

  • We will data transformation to reduce the effect of data compositionality, which can stronly bias the results.

  • Microbiome data is heavily sparsed, and thus we need to replace zeros with any meaningful value to be able to perform data transformation.

Tutorial

This part of the course is directly taken from the microViz tutorial.

Let’s proceed then:

RStudio

Statistical modelling
remotes::install_github("statdivlab/corncob")
remotes::install_github("david-barnett/microViz")
library(microViz)
library(corncob)
library(dplyr)

lm_models <- two_sample_data %>%
tax_fix() %>%
tax_prepend_ranks() %>%
# it makes sense to perform the compositional transformation BEFORE filtering
tax_transform("compositional", rank = "Order", keep_counts = TRUE) %>%
tax_filter(min_prevalence = 0.2, undetected = 0, use_counts = TRUE) %>%
taxatree_models(
    type = lm,
    trans = "log2", trans_args = list(zero_replace = "halfmin"),
    ranks = NULL, # uses every rank available except the first
    variables = c("Group")
)

lm_stats <- taxatree_models2stats(lm_models)
lm_stats %>% taxatree_stats_get()
lm_stats <- taxatree_stats_p_adjust(
data = lm_stats, method = "BH", grouping = "rank"
)

set.seed(123) # label position
key <- taxatree_plotkey(
data = lm_stats,
taxon_renamer = function(x) stringr::str_remove(x, "[PFG]: "),
# 2 lines of conditions below, for filtering taxa to be labelled
rank == "Phylum" | rank == "Order" & prevalence > 0.5,
!grepl("Kingdom", taxon)
) +
# add a bit more space for the longer labels by expanding the x axis
scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.2))
# all phyla are labelled, and all genera with a prevalence of over 0.2
# except for any taxa whose names (partly) match "Kingdom"
# (i.e. an unclassified taxon)

trees <- lm_stats %>%
taxatree_plots(
    node_size_range = c(1, 3), var_renamer = toupper
) %>%
patchwork::wrap_plots(
    ncol = 1, guides = "collect"
) 

panel <- patchwork::wrap_plots(key, trees, nrow = 1, widths = 8:7)
set.seed(111)
panel
Statistical modelling

Taxonomic tree showing which microbes are more abundant (brown) or less abundant (teal) in the Unenriched group, with the key on the left and significant taxa (p < 0.05) marked with open circles on the right.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
After having completed this chapter you will be able to:

  • Explain the principles of de novo metagenomic assembly and the algorithms (overlap–layout–consensus, de Bruijn graphs) behind the common metagenome assemblers.
  • Discuss the challenges that community complexity, strain microdiversity and uneven coverage pose for assembly, and how they translate into fragmented or chimeric contigs.
  • Evaluate assembly quality with the standard metrics and tools (contig count, N50, MetaQUAST).
  • Describe binning strategies for recovering individual genomes from assemblies, and distinguish composition-based from coverage-based (and hybrid) approaches.
  • Explain how differential coverage across samples improves binning, and how assemblers and binners are combined into workflows such as nf-core/mag.
  • Inspect the output of an end-to-end MAG-recovery pipeline and decode the naming scheme of the recovered bins.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: In this chapter we recover Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs) from the shotgun dataset introduced in Day 3 (Cuatro Ciénegas, México). Session 7 covers the theory of de novo metagenome assembly; Session 8 covers how individual genomes are carved out of the assembly (binning) and how both steps are orchestrated in a single workflow with nf-core/mag. The quality assessment, annotation and interpretation of the recovered MAGs is the topic of Day 5.

docs.title: Principles of de novo assembly
docs.text:
Assembly reconstructs the original genomes from millions of short (or long) reads, without a reference. In its simplest form the problem is solved by finding overlaps between reads and laying them out into longer contiguous sequences (contigs), a paradigm known as overlap–layout–consensus (OLC) — the basis of classic assemblers such as CAP3 or Canu/Flye for long reads.

Modern short-read assemblers instead build a de Bruijn graph: the reads are broken into k-mers (overlapping fragments of length k), which become nodes of a graph in which edges represent (k–1)-mer overlaps. Reads from the same genomic region then trace paths through the graph, and contigs are extracted as non-branching paths. This is the foundation of the metagenome assemblers we use in practice:

  • MEGAHIT — compact, fast de Bruijn graph assembler designed for large and complex metagenomes (single-end or paired-end short reads). Used in the pipeline below.
  • metaSPAdes / metaViSPAdes — multi-k de Bruijn approach with better contiguity at higher compute cost.
  • metaFlye — Flye adapted to noisy long reads; the standard choice for Nanopore/PacBio assemblies, often combined with short reads in hybrid mode.
  • hifiasm-meta — designed for high-accuracy long reads (PacBio HiFi).

docs.title: Challenges of metagenome assembly
docs.text:
Assembling a community is fundamentally harder than assembling a single genome:

  • Uneven coverage — abundant organisms assemble into long contigs, while rare members remain fragmented or unassembled altogether.
  • Strain microdiversity — closely related strains share most of their sequence; their strain-specific variants create branches in the graph and shatter assemblies (or worse, produce chimeric contigs that mix strains).
  • Community complexity — soil or marine communities contain thousands of genomes; the more complex the community, the shorter and more tangled the contigs.
  • Uneven genome characteristics — GC extremes and repeats further break contiguity.

The consequences are chimeric contigs, fragmented genomes and mis-binned sequences downstream — always keep this in mind when interpreting the length and quality distributions of what we will recover in Session 8.

docs.title: Assembly quality metrics
docs.text:
Assemblies are typically summarized with:

  • Number of contigs and total assembly size — how fragmented is the reconstruction?
  • N50 / L50 — the contig length at which 50% of the assembly is contained in contigs at least that long (a contiguity summary; not a correctness measure!).
  • Misassemblies and correctly placed bases — assessed by aligning the assembly to a reference with tools such as QUAST/MetaQUAST (when a close reference exists) or by mapping the reads back to the assembly to check consistency (e.g. with Bandage, or with the mapping statistics produced by the pipeline).
  • For the recovered genomes later on, quality is judged with completeness/contamination estimates (CheckM2, BUSCO) — the topic of Day 5.

docs.title: Session 8 - Draft genomes (bins) and Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs)
From contigs to genomes: binning strategies
docs.text:
A metagenome assembly is a soup of contigs from many organisms. Binning groups contigs into draft genomes — the MAGs. Two complementary signals drive every binner:

  • Composition — each genome has a characteristic tetranucleotide (or longer k-mer) frequency and GC content, imprinted on all of its contigs. Composition alone struggles with short contigs and with closely related strains.
  • Coverage — the abundance of a genome’s contigs should be similar. Crucially, using multiple samples (differential coverage) gives each genome a coverage profile across samples that acts as a powerful fingerprint, since different organisms fluctuate independently between samples.
  • Hybrid binners — combine both signals. The workhorses in current pipelines are MetaBAT2 and MaxBin2 (both run by nf-core/mag, which is why you will see two series of bins per sample below), with newer alternatives such as VAMB, CONCOCT and ensemble refinements such as DAS Tool that reconcile the outputs of several binners.

How to get better bins

Sequence several samples that share members of the community (differential coverage!), aim for sufficient depth (Day 3), and refine/consensus-bin the outputs of multiple binners rather than trusting a single one.

docs.title: nf-core/mag: assembly and binning in one workflow
docs.text:
The pipeline used to build the MAGs was nf-core/mag, a Nextflow workflow that chains quality control and host-read removal, assembly (MEGAHIT and/or metaSPAdes), binning (MetaBAT2, MaxBin2), bin refinement, and downstream genome annotation and quality control (Prokka, CheckM). The usage of the pipeline can be checked here, and below is the workflow it follows:

nf-core/mag workflow used to assemble the sequencing reads and recover the MAGs.

Since running the pipeline demands high computational resources, we have pre-computed it for you on the same nine samples used in Day 3 (you can find the commands to execute nf-core/mag on the Moodle page as Commands to run nf-core/mag and MAGFlow). In the hands-on below we explore its outputs, and we decode what the pipeline produced.

docs.title: Hands-on: exploring the recovered MAGs
docs.text:
If not done already, login to your GitHub account and open the Codespaces training environment opening this link in a new tab:

https://codespaces.new/nextflow-io/training?quickstart=1&ref=2.1.5

The pre-computed results are placed within the metagenomics directory of the workspace (data/faas/ contains the predicted proteins per MAG; download and extract the folder intermediate.tar.gz from the Moodle page for the GenBank annotations and the remaining outputs used on Day 5).

docs.title: 1. Look at the recovered MAGs
docs.text:
The protein FASTA files (.faa, produced by Prokka) are named after the sample, the assembler and the binning tool. List them and count how many MAGs were recovered per binner:

List the MAGs recovered by the pipeline
cd data/faas

# how many MAGs in total?
ls *.faa | wc -l

# how many per binning tool?
ls *.faa | grep MetaBAT2 | wc -l
ls *.faa | grep MaxBin2 | wc -l

# which samples contributed MAGs?
ls *.faa | sed 's/\..*//' | sort -u

Question

Do both binners recover the same number of MAGs per sample? What does this tell you about the (dis)agreement between composition- and coverage-based binning?

docs.title: 2. Decode the naming scheme
docs.text:
Understand the file naming
# the pattern is: ASSEMBLER-BINNER-SAMPLE.BIN.faa
# e.g. MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.faa
#   -> assembled with MEGAHIT, binned with MetaBAT2,
#      from sample ERR2143759, bin number 7

ls MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-*.faa
ls MEGAHIT-MaxBin2-*.faa

docs.title: 3. Inspect the content of one MAG
docs.text:
Peek into a MAG
# how many proteins were predicted in this MAG?
grep -c '^>' MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.faa

# look at the predicted proteins (amino-acid sequences)
head -20 MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.faa

Each of these files is a draft genome: a set of genes recovered from the community without ever culturing its organism. The GenBank version of the same MAG (with genes annotated on the contigs) is found at intermediate/gbks/MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.gbk — we will use it on Day 5 for visualization and secondary-metabolite detection.

docs.title: 4. Relate bins to their contigs
docs.text:
MEGAHIT names contigs with short random-looking codes. The mapping between each MAG and its contig name is provided in the following file (download):

Map bins to contigs
head ../summary_contigs.tsv
Bin Contig name MEGAHIT-MaxBin2-ERR2143759.001.tsv GIFAEIHF MEGAHIT-MaxBin2-ERR2143759.002.tsv CIJAKMNO MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.tsv KKNACEHJ

(A subset of the full table is shown above; the complete mapping is in the downloadable file.) This kind of bookkeeping matters when you go back from a downstream result (e.g. “this MAG degrades cellulose”) to the actual sequences that support it.

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
Questions

  • Which samples yielded MAGs, and which did not? Given what you learned in Session 7, what could explain this?
  • Why are there two series of bins (MetaBAT2 and MaxBin2) for the same assembly? Would you trust one binner over the other, and how could you decide?
  • What are the limitations of the MAGs we just recovered (completeness, contamination, strain chimerism)? How would you quantify them?

These last questions lead us directly to Day 5, where we assess the quality of these MAGs, annotate their functions and discuss how to make such analyses FAIR and reproducible.

docs.title: Day 5 - MAG quality assessment, annotation and FAIR data
Learning outcomes
docs.text:
After having completed this chapter you will be able to:

  • Evaluate the completeness and contamination of MAGs with BUSCO and CheckM2, and relate the results to quality standards (e.g. MIMAG) for reporting draft genomes.
  • Classify MAGs taxonomically and assess their quality and taxonomy interactively with the MAGFlow/BIgMAG dashboard.
  • Infer the metabolic potential of MAGs from KEGG orthology terms with KEGG Decoder.
  • Annotate and compare functional categories with COGclassifier, dbCAN3 (CAZymes) and antiSMASH (biosynthetic gene clusters).
  • Visualize and annotate prokaryotic genomes with Proksee, and compare the gene repertoire of related MAGs with a pangenome analysis (Roary/Phandango).

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: In the previous chapters we classified communities at the read level (Day 3) and recovered draft genomes from the assembly (Day 4). This final chapter closes the analysis arc: in Session 9 we assess, annotate and interpret the MAGs recovered with nf-core/mag, and in Session 10 we zoom out to the principles that let you (and others) reuse everything you have just done: FAIR data and reproducible workflows.

docs.title: Session 9 - MAG quality assessment, annotation and classification
From bins to trustworthy genomes
docs.text:
A bin is just a set of contigs that a binner believes belong together. Before a MAG can be reported or interpreted biologically, three questions must be answered:

  • Completeness — how much of the genome is present? Estimated from the recovery of ubiquitous single-copy marker genes (BUSCO, CheckM2).
  • Contamination — how much foreign sequence has been binned along with it? Detected as unexpected duplications of those same marker genes.
  • Taxonomy — which organism does the genome belong to? Derived from marker-gene phylogenies, typically with the GTDB taxonomy.

These criteria are formalized in the MIMAG (Minimum Information about a Metagenome-Assembled Genome) standards, which define quality tiers (e.g. “high-quality” draft: >90% completeness, <5% contamination, plus rRNA/tRNA requirements) that journals increasingly expect when MAGs are reported.

docs.title: MAGFlow/BIgMAG
docs.text:
MAGFlow is a tool designed to combine several tools to measure the quality of the bins/MAGs, as well as to taxonomically annotate them. This is the workflow:

MAGFlow workflow used to assess the quality and taxonomic annotation of the MAGs.

The output of this tool is a ready-to-use file that concatenates the results, and it can then be used as input for BIgMAG. We will not execute MAGFlow today (you can find the commands to execute MAGFlow on the Moodle page as Commands to run nf-core/mag and MAGFlow), and hence you will find the final_df.tsv within intermediate/magflow/ (download and extract the folder intermediate.tar.gz from the Moodle page) to display the BIgMAG dashboard. Let’s create then the environment for BIgMAG by running the following commands on the GitHub Codespaces terminal:

Set up the BIgMAG environment
git clone https://github.com/jeffe107/BIgMAG
conda create -n BIgMAG --file BIgMAG/requirements.txt
conda activate BIgMAG

Whenever you are asked whether to install extra packages

Please say yes to all!

Now, we are ready to execute BIgMAG to perform the exploratory analysis of the MAG overall quality and annotation:

Run the BIgMAG dashboard
BIgMAG/app.py -p 8050 data/magflow/final_df.tsv

You will see on the terminal a link to the dashboard or the editor will offer you an option to directly open a new tab on the browser, just click on it.

Now, it is your turn to analyze the results, use these questions to guide your thoughts:

BIgMAG - overall quality

Overall, the MAGs recovered within your assigned samples have good quality? What would you suggest to improve the quality of the bins that do not depict enough quality?

BIgMAG - quality metrics

The results displayed by BUSCO and CheckM2 are correspondent? Why do you think this is happening?

BIgMAG - taxonomy

Stop the dashboard

Do not forget to stop the dashboard with Ctrl + c, and to deactivate the environment with:

Deactivate the BIgMAG environment

docs.title: KEGG Decoder
docs.text:
Moving forward, it is time now to identify genomic features within the bins/MAGs. KEGG Decoder is a tool that interprets the metabolic potential of the MAGs (or any genome in general) by analyzing the presence of KEGG Orthology (KO) identifiers. It maps these KOs to major metabolic pathways (biogeochemically relevant) and summarizes the completeness of each pathway based on predefined modules. Being so, we can infer the metabolic capabilities of the community, and gain insights into functional differences across samples or MAGs.

Prokka (included within nf-core/mag) has provided us with the annotation about the presence/localization of enzymes in the bins/MAGs that are involved in a wide variety of processes. Nonetheless, Prokka uses EC numbers to describe such genomic features, and as a result, we needed to transform these annotations to K numbers and merge them into a single file (this was already done for you, the required files to perform these translations can be found within the directory stored on the Moodle page as additional_files.tar.gz). Now, let’s install KEGG Decoder:

Install KEGG Decoder
conda create -n keggdecoder python=3.6
conda activate keggdecoder
python3 -m pip install KEGGDecoder

Whenever you are asked whether to install extra packages

Please say yes to all!

Now, we are ready to execute this software to determine the presence and completeness of the annotated metabolic pathways:

Run KEGG Decoder
KEGG-decoder --input data/k_numbers/megahit_k_numbers.tsv --output kegg_output.tsv --vizoption static

This command will create a heatmap where you can perform a comparison across MAGs. In this case, we are analyzing the MAGs obtained with the assembler MEGAHIT. It should look like this:

docs.title: COG Annotation
docs.text:
Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COGs) are groups of genes from different organisms that evolved from a common ancestral gene and retain the same function. To explore these genes, we rely on the amino-acid sequences of the coding regions provided by Prokka (.faa files). The next task, then, will be to install a COGclassifier in order to detect Clusters of Ortholog Genes:

Install COGclassifier
conda create -n cogclassifier -c conda-forge -c bioconda cogclassifier
conda activate cogclassifier

Whenever you are asked whether to install extra packages

Please say yes to all!

This tool automatically performs the processes from searching query sequences into the COG database, to annotation and classification of gene functions, to generation of publication-ready figures. However, the input for this tool is only one genome each time. This does not mean that we cannot analyze all the bins/MAGs; we could simply execute the software for each of them and integrate the data afterwards. To launch the tool just run on the terminal:

Run COGclassifier
COGclassifier -i data/faas/MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.faa -o cog_annotation --download_dir ./cog_database

Once it has finished, inside cog_annotation you will see the output represented as tables featuring counts, summary and annotations, as well as interesting figures showcasing the proportion of the different COG categories, just like this:

COGclassifier figure showcasing the proportion of the different COG categories for one MAG.

COG categories

What are the categories that are more representative of this MAG? Do you see any odd results?

COG comparisons

If you decide to analyze all of the MAGs, do you think it would be a fair comparison just using the raw counts obtained by the software? If not, what strategy would you propose to proceed further?

Deactivate the environment

Do not forget to deactivate the environment with:

Deactivate the cogclassifier environment
conda deactivate

docs.title: dbCAN3
docs.text:
CAZymes (Carbohydrate-Active enZymes) are enzymes involved in the breakdown, biosynthesis, or modification of carbohydrates and glycoconjugates. They play a crucial role in processing complex carbohydrates such as cellulose, hemicellulose, starch, and chitin, among others. To detect the presence of this kind of enzymes, we are going to use the tool dbCAN3, which is an automated web server designed to run the software and provide the results.

To execute the tool, you just need to download the file from Codespaces data/faas/MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.faa, upload it to the server (click here), submit a job and wait for the results.

Tools included in the execution

You can select the tools to include in the execution (HMMER, DIAMOND, dbCAN-sub, CGCFinder). However, please keep in mind that the more tools you include, the longer the run.

docs.title: antiSMASH
docs.text:
antiSMASH (antibiotics & Secondary Metabolite Analysis SHell) is a tool that detects and analyzes biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) in microbial genomes. These clusters are groups of co-located genes that together encode the machinery to produce secondary metabolites—specialized compounds that are not essential for basic cellular functions.

Analogous to dbCAN3, we will use the web server to annotate one of the MAGs recovered by the pipeline. Upload the file intermediate/gbks/MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.gbk (download and extract the folder intermediate.tar.gz from the Moodle page) to antiSMASH and wait for the results.

If it takes some time, we have performed this step for you and we stored the results within the same intermediate.tar.gz file, at intermediate/antiSMASH/index.html.

docs.title: Proksee
docs.text:
Proksee is an interactive web-based tool for visualizing, annotating, and analyzing prokaryotic genomes. Using this tool we can visualize genomes as circular or linear maps, annotate them, customize the visualization and export high-level and detailed-oriented figures.

Same as with previous applications, you just need to upload the annotated genome in FASTA or GenBank format. Here, we are going to leverage the files produced by Prokka, and hence you just need to upload the file (download and extract the folder intermediate.tar.gz from the Moodle page) intermediate/gbks/MEGAHIT-MetaBAT2-ERR2143759.7.gbk to Proksee.

You can customize the display, add features, re-annotate the genome among many other functionalities. Unfortunately, it processes only one genome at a time. From here it’s up to your goals/motivation to take advantage of this tool.

You should be seeing this example:

Proksee circular map visualizing the annotated genome of one of the MAGs.

docs.title: Pangenome
docs.text:
For the past tools we have not analyzed just a random MAG: we selected this one given that its taxonomic annotation is shared across different samples (from the BIgMAG exercise), and therefore it is interesting to establish the similarities/differences among these MAGs to enable a pangenome analysis. In this case, we study the entire gene repertoire of related MAGs (same species or genus); for our analysis we have selected some MAGs based on GTDB classification.

Next, we run the tool Roary that determines the core genome, accessory genome and unique genome. We have pre-computed the results for you following the tutorial presented by the developers of the tool, and now we are going to visualize the results using Phandango.

Drag and drop the files (download and extract the folder intermediate.tar.gz from the Moodle page) intermediate/pangenome/JAAUTG01/workshop.newick and intermediate/pangenome/JAAUTG01/gene_presence_absence.csv to the Phandango web server and visualize the results.

It should look like this:

Phandango output visualizing the Roary pangenome analysis of the selected MAGs.

Usually, this analysis is carried out using a reference genome; however, given that these MAGs are not annotated at species level, and genus annotation is not informative, we do not count with a reference genome to explore the pangenome of these MAGs. You can visualize an example that includes a reference genome with the files found at intermediate/pangenome/example_with_reference (download and extract the folder intermediate.tar.gz from the Moodle page).

docs.title: Why FAIR?
docs.text:
Everything we did in this course produces valuable research objects: raw reads, assemblies, MAGs, taxonomy tables, figures. If these outputs cannot be found, accessed, interoperated and reused — by your future self, by your collaborators, or by reviewers — much of their value is lost. The FAIR principles provide the checklist:

  • Findable — with a persistent identifier (DOI/accession) and rich, indexed metadata.
  • Accessible — deposited in a trusted repository, retrievable with standard protocols (and clear license/conditions).
  • Interoperable — using community formats and controlled vocabularies/ontologies, so that both humans and machines can process the data.
  • Reusable — with clear provenance (how the data were generated and processed) and a license that states how it may be reused.

docs.title: FAIR in practice: repositories and metadata
docs.text:
For metagenomics, this translates into concrete actions:

  • Raw reads — deposited in INSDC repositories (NCBI SRA, ENA, DDBJ) at submission of the associated BioProject/BioSample. Note that the datasets used in this course (PRJNA256993 on Day 2, PRJEB22811 on Day 3) are public exactly because they were submitted with proper metadata.
  • Metadata — follow the community checklists: MIxS (Genomic Standards Consortium) packages for environment, host and sampling metadata; MIMAG for MAG reports (quality metrics, taxonomy, code availability). Metadata richness is what makes the difference between a reusable dataset and an uninterpretable FASTQ file.
  • Assemblies and MAGs — deposited in GenBank/IMG-M/ MG-RAST with their quality statistics and taxonomy.
  • Analysis outputs and code — supplementary tables with DOIs (e.g. Zenodo, connected to a GitHub release), plus the exact commands and parameters used.

Question

Look at the PRJNA256993_SraRunTable.txt metadata you used on Day 2: which MIxS fields are covered? Which ones would a reviewer still ask for (e.g. sampling protocol, extraction kit, PCR primers)?

docs.title: Reproducible analyses: workflows and containers
docs.text:
FAIR data alone is not enough: the process that turns reads into results must also be reproducible. Throughout this course we have (implicitly and explicitly) relied on the two pillars of computational reproducibility in bioinformatics:

  • Workflow managers — tools such as Nextflow (used for the Kraken2/Bracken pipeline on Day 3 and for nf-core/mag on Day 4) capture the entire analysis — every tool, parameter, input and output — in a single executable, versioned definition that can run on a laptop, a cluster or the cloud. Communities such as nf-core provide curated, peer-reviewed workflows that you can reuse instead of reinventing.
  • Containers — Docker/Singularity images freeze the software environment (OS libraries, tool versions) of each step, so the same workflow produces the same result anywhere, forever. nf-core pipelines, for example, ship every process as a container.

A practical recipe for a FAIR and reproducible metagenomics analysis:

  1. Version your workflow and scripts in Git (e.g. on GitHub), with a README that states how to run them.
  2. Run them with a workflow manager (Nextflow, Snakemake) using containers/conda environments pinned to specific versions.
  3. Record the parameters and database versions (e.g. the exact Kraken2 database and Silva release used above).
  4. Deposit raw data and derived objects in trusted repositories with rich metadata and persistent identifiers.
  5. Report according to community standards (MIxS, MIMAG), and license your code and data so others can reuse them.

docs.title: Course wrap-up
docs.text:
Over these five days you have travelled the full metagenomics analysis arc: from study design and quality control (Day 1), through targeted amplicon analysis (Day 2), read-based shotgun classification and community statistics (Day 3), de novo assembly and MAG recovery (Day 4), to MAG quality assessment and functional interpretation (Session 9) — and finally to the principles that make all of it shareable and reusable (this session). We hope you will take this workflow back to your own data!

Post-course support

You will receive continued support via email for 30 days following the course, along with on-demand access to the session recordings for the same period. Do not hesitate to bring your own data questions to the discussion slots or by email.
